description: I'm Akshata, a network operations engineer , curious about the brain and AI — how we stay calm under pressure and reach our full potential. I picked the Interplanetary Survival Guide challenge: building an AI survival coach that trains astronauts' minds for Mars — stress, panic, calm decisions. I bring engineering experience and a passion for the human mind.
summary: A Mars map that plans a safe multi-day trip to Mount Sharp — and when a dust storm hits during one walk, a calm AI coach (three scripted lines) helps the astronaut breathe, check one thing, decide one thing, and follow the safe route home. It layers three kinds of NASA data — Mars Trek pictures, MOLA heights, and Mars climate data — across Gale Crater, where the Curiosity rover landed and still explores, to reach the boxwork formations: rock walls built by water long ago. A route-planning program scores candidate paths; the route was chosen because it visits the science stops. The trip is 33.1 km in three measured legs — START to Boxwork 9.3 km, Boxwork to High ground 21.0 km, High ground to Mount Sharp 2.8 km — with a total climb of 4,991 m. NASA's maps guide robots. Ours guides a scared person.
details:
Astronauts on Mars must walk outside to do science. Two things can go wrong: the ground — rocks and steep slopes — and the mind — panic when something goes wrong. Our project helps with both, in one place.

Try it yourself — the interactive map: https://muse.ai/s/marswalk-coach-map-xvxx6ixpr0kuc7/6ISh8tnLEI6YA2V27dYyA5fMcSWeStl5XputRSvuewM — you can walk the route, see the mountain and the storm in 3D, read the danger list, and see how the routes scored.

Meet the coach: Breathe–Check–Decide. In our story, a dust storm rises early in one day's walk, a short walk from the landing-site base. The alarm sounds. Panic starts. Earth is up to 20 minutes away by radio, so no help can come from home in time. That is why the coach lives on the map, right where the astronaut is. NASA research says CapCom's job — the calm voice that guides astronauts — must move onto Mars. Our coach is a small piece of that idea, in three short lines: breathe with me — check one thing on the map — decide one thing now. Then the astronaut follows the white dashes home. The full coach guide is in the repo (COACH_GUIDE.md). Our next step: the guide in VR glasses, reading the astronaut's cues, so the coach knows when to speak without being asked.

The map plans the trip. The map shows Gale Crater and Mount Sharp, from NASA Mars Trek. One safe route is drawn for the whole trip: 33.1 km over several days, in three measured parts — START to Boxwork 9.3 km, Boxwork to High ground 21.0 km, High ground to Mount Sharp 2.8 km. The total climb is 4,991 m. Our story follows one walk on one day of this trip. Three real dangers are marked — a crater, rough ground, and a steep slope — plus one more the map learned in a demo. On the map, the dangers sit near the route so you can see the idea; their real positions are approximate, 20 to 40 km from the safe corridor.

How we know the route is good. We built a small program (Python, in the repo) that scores three possible routes with three plain rules: dangers crossed, length, and climb. Our route's climb comes from real NASA MOLA height numbers we sampled ourselves; the other two routes use stated climb classes. Our route wins with 4 points, tied with the wide detour and winning because it is shorter. We are honest about the scoring: the other two routes were scored by eye, and when our second program (Weighted A*) measured the straight line, it found zero danger crossings — measured the same way, the straight line would score 5. So the score alone does not pick our route. The science stops do — the straight line skips them. A third program uses Field D*, the routing method NASA flew on its rovers. It plans through the science stops, finds the gentlest path around steep slopes (35.0 km), and when a new rock field appears, it makes a new plan by rechecking only 4% of the states. It scores 3 points only because its climb is 3 metres over the 5,000 m line — the simple scorer does not reward gentle. When Field D* finds a new danger, the map remembers it, so the next walk avoids it from the start. The danger list behind all this holds the 3 real dangers — the crater and rough ground checked by eye on the Mars Trek map, with real Curiosity Hazcam ground photos confirming the rough-ground type — plus the 1 demo-learned one.

Safety and honest limits. One safety rule is built into the climb chart: turn back before you are halfway, while you still have the air and the light to get home. And honestly: this is a planning guide and a scripted coach, not a live tracker. The storm readings on the map are simulated, not live.

The ending is quiet. The astronaut is back safe. The last line says: "A calm mind is survival equipment."

Tools used: Python (route scorer, A* planner, and Field D* planner), NASA Mars Trek (map), Google Slides (demo deck), PIL (drawing the route on the map images). The demo is the 7-slide deck.
